routes.description: Establish that Catholic theism can reconcile hiddenness, unequal religious conditions, sincere nonbelief, hell, and original sin with universal grace by combining providential formation, meaningful creaturely agency, differentiated goods, and humanity's recoverable loss of gratuitous gifts.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if universal access to sufficient grace remains coherent despite unequal explicit revelation, responsible refusal remains possible without treating belief as directly voluntary, and inherited fallen conditions can be explained without attributing arbitrary punishment or divine abandonment.

motionBridge.description: Show that grace, providence, and creaturely agency jointly explain the motion's apparent counterevidence without denying its unequal and painful manifestations.

centralBridges.description: Account for sincere nonbelief and religious geography while maintaining that every person receives a genuinely sufficient path toward God.
Explain how providentially supplied opportunities can coexist with finite interpretation, temporal development, contingency, and meaningful refusal.
Explain original sin as the loss of gratuitous gifts through shared human rejection while preserving the availability of restoration.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Relate unequal natural, cultural, and revelatory conditions to differentiated personal and communal goods rather than uniform distribution.
Show how scriptural narrative and suffering can form receptivity to revelation within a larger providential history.

routes.description: Establish that persistent sincere nonbelief, culturally patterned revelation, unequal salvific costs, hell, and inherited fallen conditions are less expected under a loving God who seeks relationship with everyone than under explanations centered on human culture and contingency.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the proposed appeals to grace, providence, agency, differentiated goods, and original sin do not adequately explain failed divine contact, unequal access and eternal stakes, rationally involuntary rejection, or inherited deprivation following deception.

motionBridge.description: Show that the combined pattern of hiddenness, unequal geography, sincere nonbelief, hell, and original sin counts against Catholic theism.

centralBridges.description: Establish that sincere seekers can remain without reciprocal divine contact despite willingness to know and relate to God.
Connect geographic and social disparities in revelation to unequal intellectual, practical, and potentially eternal consequences.
Challenge whether nonbelief, rejection of salvation, or primordial disobedience can bear the required culpability under ignorance, cognitive limitation, or deception.
Challenge whether solidarity with primordial humanity can justify inherited deprivation and suffering for later persons.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Test whether contingent encounters, interrupted lives, and providential orchestration can be reconciled with both fair access and creaturely freedom.
Test whether appeals to a larger divine story explain severe suffering and withheld explanation consistently with divine love.

sections.title: Divine Hiddenness and Sincere Seeking
sections.rationale: This issue tests the central relational question: whether persistent nonbelief among willing seekers is compatible with universal divine availability and a life-spanning process of revelation and formation.

sections.title: Religious Geography, Unequal Access, and Fairness
sections.rationale: This issue connects culturally uneven belief and differing social costs to the competing expectations of universal divine concern, differentiated providence, and sociological transmission.

sections.title: Grace, Responsible Refusal, and Hell
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether sufficient grace and meaningful agency can ground responsibility for rejecting salvation when belief is not directly voluntary and the consequences are eternal.

sections.title: Providence, Mortal Contingency, and Transformative Suffering
sections.rationale: This issue examines whether interrupted lives, contingent encounters, and suffering can belong to a coherent providential history without making access arbitrary or compromising creaturely agency.

sections.title: Original Sin, Deception, Solidarity, and Restoration
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether the fall can coherently explain humanity's inherited condition through lost gratuitous gifts and shared nature despite objections concerning deception, culpability, and intergenerational justice.
